question: What is the short title given to RPL Article 14 by Section 460?
choice_a: The New York State Property Condition Disclosure Act
choice_b: The New York Truth in Housing Act
choice_c: The Residential Seller Disclosure Act
choice_d: The New York Home Inspection Act
explanation: RPL 460 gives Article 14 the short title "the property condition disclosure act."

question: Under RPL 461, how is "agent" defined for purposes of Article 14?
choice_a: Any person who assists in the sale of a home, licensed or not
choice_b: A real estate broker or salesperson licensed under RPL Article 12-A who is acting in a fiduciary capacity in the transaction
choice_c: Only an attorney representing the seller
choice_d: A title company representative who handles the closing
explanation: Section 461 defines "agent" as a licensed real estate broker or salesperson acting under RPL 440-a in a fiduciary capacity for a party to the transaction.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four categories of "real estate purchase contract" defined in RPL 461?
choice_a: A standard contract for the purchase and sale of residential real property
choice_b: A lease containing an option to purchase the residential real property
choice_c: A residential lease containing no option or obligation to purchase the property
choice_d: An installment land contract for residential real property
explanation: Section 461 defines "real estate purchase contract" to cover standard purchase/sale agreements, leases with a purchase option, leases with an obligation to purchase, and installment land contracts -- a plain lease with no purchase option or obligation is not one of the four categories.

question: Under RPL 461, when does a "transfer of title" occur for purposes of Article 14?
choice_a: Only when the deed is recorded in the county clerk's office
choice_b: Only at the moment the buyer takes physical possession
choice_c: Only when the mortgage lender disburses loan proceeds
choice_d: Upon delivery of a properly executed instrument conveying the residential real property, including delivery of a lease or installment land contract covered by the Article
explanation: Section 461 defines "transfer of title" as delivery of a properly executed conveyance instrument for residential real property, including delivery of purchase contracts that are leases or installment contracts covered by the Article.

question: How does RPL 461 define a "binding contract of sale"?
choice_a: A purchase contract or offer that would obligate the buyer to accept title upon the seller's signature and satisfaction of any contingencies
choice_b: Any signed listing agreement between a seller and a broker
choice_c: The final deed transferring title at closing
choice_d: A letter of intent that is non-binding on both parties
explanation: Section 461 defines "binding contract of sale" as a purchase contract or offer that would obligate the buyer to accept title once signed by the seller and any contingencies are satisfied.

question: A seller is transferring a five-family residential building. Is a Property Condition Disclosure Statement required under RPL Article 14?
choice_a: Yes, because all residential income property is covered
choice_b: No, because Article 14 only covers dwellings improved with a one to four family residence
choice_c: Yes, but only if fewer than three units are owner-occupied
choice_d: No, but only because the building lacks a certificate of occupancy
explanation: RPL 461 defines "residential real property" as property improved by a one to four family dwelling used or occupied as a home or residence; a five-family building falls outside that definition entirely.

question: Which of these items would typically be addressed in the "general information" section of the Property Condition Disclosure Statement under RPL 462?
choice_a: The buyer's projected loan-to-value ratio
choice_b: The seller's asking price history on the open market
choice_c: Whether a certificate of occupancy has been issued for the dwelling and any known easements affecting the property
choice_d: The commission rate charged by the seller's broker
explanation: The general information portion of the RPL 462 disclosure form covers items such as certificate of occupancy status, easements, ownership duration, and title claims -- not brokerage or financing terms.

question: Which of these items would also fall under the "general information" section of the Property Condition Disclosure Statement under RPL 462?
choice_a: The current mortgage interest rate available to the buyer
choice_b: The seller's brokerage commission split with the buyer's broker
choice_c: The projected date the buyer's mortgage contingency expires
choice_d: Whether the property shares any features, such as walls, driveways, or roads, in undivided common ownership with an adjoining property
explanation: The general information section of the RPL 462 form also covers shared or undivided-ownership features like common walls, driveways, or roads with adjoining properties.

question: Which of these is a structural disclosure item on the Property Condition Disclosure Statement under RPL 462?
choice_a: The age and condition of the roof, and any known water or wood-rot damage
choice_b: The interest rate on the seller's existing mortgage
choice_c: The date the property was last appraised
choice_d: Whether the seller used a real estate attorney at closing
explanation: The structural section of the RPL 462 disclosure form covers items such as roof age and condition, water or wood-rot damage, fire damage, and foundation defects.

question: Which of these would also be addressed under the structural section of the Property Condition Disclosure Statement per RPL 462?
choice_a: The property's current real estate tax assessment
choice_b: Known infestation by wood-destroying insects or organisms
choice_c: The buyer's proposed occupancy date
choice_d: The seller's homeowner association dues history
explanation: The structural section of the RPL 462 disclosure form also covers known infestation by wood-destroying insects or organisms, alongside roof, foundation, and water/fire damage items.

question: Which item is covered under the "mechanical systems and services" portion of the Property Condition Disclosure Statement per RPL 462?
choice_a: The seller's marginal income tax bracket
choice_b: The buyer's homeowners insurance premium
choice_c: The source of the dwelling's water supply and the type of sewage disposal system
choice_d: The zoning classification of neighboring parcels
explanation: The mechanical systems and services section of the RPL 462 form covers water source, sewage disposal type, electrical service, HVAC, plumbing, and safety devices like smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.

question: In addition to flood-related items, which of these is an environmental disclosure item on the Property Condition Disclosure Statement per RPL 462?
choice_a: The buyer's flood insurance premium quote
choice_b: The seller's homeowners insurance claims history unrelated to flooding
choice_c: The buyer's proposed renovation plans
choice_d: Known presence of asbestos, lead in plumbing, or elevated radon levels
explanation: The environmental section of the RPL 462 form covers items such as asbestos, lead plumbing, radon, wetlands, agricultural districts, landfills, and fuel storage tanks, in addition to floodplain and flood-insurance items.

question: According to RPL 462, what is the legal effect of the Property Condition Disclosure Statement on a buyer's right to obtain an independent home inspection?
choice_a: The statement has no effect on that right -- it is not a substitute for, and does not replace, an independent inspection
choice_b: It waives the buyer's right to any further inspection
choice_c: It replaces the need for inspection, but only for structural items
choice_d: It obligates the buyer to use the seller's own inspector
explanation: RPL 462 provides that the Disclosure Statement is not a warranty and is not a substitute for any inspections or professional advice the buyer may wish to obtain.

question: Under RPL 465, what happens if a seller fails to deliver a Property Condition Disclosure Statement to the buyer before the buyer signs a binding contract of sale?
choice_a: The contract of sale automatically becomes void
choice_b: The buyer is entitled to a credit of $500 against the agreed purchase price at the transfer of title
choice_c: The seller forfeits the right to receive any deposit
choice_d: The Department of State may suspend the seller's ability to sell property for one year
explanation: RPL 465 provides that if a seller does not deliver a Disclosure Statement before the buyer signs a binding contract of sale, the buyer receives a fixed $500 credit against the purchase price upon transfer of title -- a distinctively New York remedy verified independently against the statutory text.

question: Why do many New York sellers of residential real property choose not to complete a Property Condition Disclosure Statement at all?
choice_a: Because RPL Article 14 makes the statement entirely optional for every seller regardless of delivery
choice_b: Because completing the statement requires a licensed home inspector's signature
choice_c: Non-delivery limits the buyer's remedy to a fixed $500 credit at closing, which many sellers view as cheaper and lower-risk than completing the form and being exposed to liability for willful misstatements
choice_d: Because the $500 credit is paid by New York State, not the seller
explanation: hedge: this reflects common real estate practice built on RPL 465's fixed $500 credit remedy for non-delivery -- widely reported in NY real estate practice guidance -- rather than an explicit statutory statement that sellers should skip disclosure.

question: A seller who DOES deliver a completed Property Condition Disclosure Statement, versus a seller who delivers none at all, faces what different standard under RPL 465?
choice_a: Both sellers face identical liability limited to the $500 credit
choice_b: The seller who delivers a statement faces strict liability for any inaccuracy, while the non-disclosing seller faces no consequence at all
choice_c: Only the non-disclosing seller can be sued for actual damages
choice_d: The seller who delivers a statement is liable only for a willful failure to perform the Article's requirements, while a seller who delivers no statement at all exposes the buyer only to the fixed $500 credit remedy
explanation: RPL 465 draws a distinction: a seller who provides (or revises) a statement is liable only for willful failure to perform, recoverable as actual damages, while a seller who delivers no statement before contract signing exposes the buyer only to the fixed $500 credit.

question: A seller has actual knowledge of a recurring basement flooding problem but deliberately marks "no known defects" on the Property Condition Disclosure Statement to help the sale close faster. Under RPL 465, what is the buyer's likely remedy?
choice_a: Actual damages, since the seller's deliberate omission of a known defect is a willful failure to perform the Article's disclosure requirements
choice_b: Only the fixed $500 credit, the same as if no statement had been delivered at all
choice_c: No remedy, since the statement was still timely delivered before contract signing
choice_d: Automatic rescission of the contract of sale
explanation: Because the seller delivered a statement but knowingly misrepresented a defect, this is a willful failure to perform under RPL 465, entitling the buyer to actual damages rather than merely the $500 non-delivery credit.

question: Which of the following transfers is exempt from the Property Condition Disclosure Statement requirement under RPL 463 as a court-ordered transfer?
choice_a: A transfer through a standard multiple listing service sale
choice_b: A transfer pursuant to a probate proceeding, a bankruptcy proceeding, or an order of specific performance
choice_c: A transfer financed with an FHA-insured mortgage
choice_d: A transfer negotiated through a real estate broker's exclusive listing
explanation: RPL 463 exempts court-ordered transfers, including those arising from probate, bankruptcy, eminent domain, and orders of specific performance, among its 14 exempt categories.

question: A lender takes title to a residential property through a deed in lieu of foreclosure and later resells it. Is that resale by the lender exempt from Article 14's disclosure requirement?
choice_a: No, lenders reselling foreclosed property are treated the same as any other individual seller
choice_b: Yes, but only if the lender is a federally chartered bank
choice_c: Yes, transfers by a mortgagee who acquired the property through foreclosure or a deed in lieu of foreclosure are among the exempt categories
choice_d: No, the exemption applies only to the original foreclosure transfer, not the lender's later resale
explanation: RPL 463 exempts transfers by a mortgagee or beneficiary who acquired the property at a mortgage foreclosure sale or through a deed in lieu of foreclosure.

question: An executor sells a decedent's residential property as part of administering the estate. Is a Property Condition Disclosure Statement required under RPL 463?
choice_a: Yes, executors have the same disclosure duty as any individual seller
choice_b: No, but only if all heirs consent in writing
choice_c: Yes, unless the estate is insolvent
choice_d: No, transfers by a fiduciary in the course of administering an estate, guardianship, conservatorship, or trust are exempt
explanation: RPL 463 exempts transfers by a fiduciary administering an estate, guardianship, conservatorship, or trust from the Disclosure Statement requirement.

question: Which of the following transfers is exempt from the Property Condition Disclosure Statement requirement under RPL 463?
choice_a: A transfer to or from the state of New York, a political subdivision, or another governmental entity
choice_b: A transfer to a first-time homebuyer using a state down-payment assistance grant
choice_c: A transfer where the buyer is a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: A transfer of a property enrolled in a co-op conversion plan
explanation: RPL 463's exempt categories include transfers involving the state of New York, its political subdivisions, or other governmental entities.

question: Which of the following is among the 14 exempt transfer categories listed in RPL 463?
choice_a: A transfer between unrelated buyers found through an online listing
choice_b: A transfer by a sheriff pursuant to court process, and a transfer made pursuant to a partition action
choice_c: A transfer where the buyer waives a home inspection contingency
choice_d: A transfer financed entirely with cash
explanation: RPL 463 lists transfers by a sheriff and transfers pursuant to a partition action among its 14 exempt categories.

question: A parent transfers residential real property to their adult child as a gift. Under RPL 463, is a Property Condition Disclosure Statement required?
choice_a: Yes, gift transfers are always covered since no purchase price is paid
choice_b: No, but only if the property is transferred by will rather than during the parent's lifetime
choice_c: No, transfers to a spouse or a lineal consanguinity relative of the transferor are exempt
choice_d: Yes, unless the child is also a licensed real estate agent
explanation: RPL 463 exempts transfers to a spouse or a lineal-consanguinity relative of the transferor(s) from the Disclosure Statement requirement, regardless of whether the transfer is a gift.

question: Under RPL 464, what triggers a seller's duty to deliver a revised Property Condition Disclosure Statement?
choice_a: Any change in the seller's asking price
choice_b: The buyer's request for a second walkthrough
choice_c: A minor, non-material change in the condition of the property
choice_d: The seller acquires actual knowledge that renders a previously delivered statement materially inaccurate
explanation: RPL 464 requires revision only when the seller acquires knowledge that makes a previously delivered statement materially inaccurate -- a minor or non-material change does not trigger the duty.

question: Once a seller's duty to revise the Disclosure Statement under RPL 464 is triggered, when must the revised statement be delivered?
choice_a: As soon as practicable, but never later than the earlier of transfer of title or buyer occupancy
choice_b: Within 24 hours of discovering the new information
choice_c: At any time before the closing, with no specific deadline
choice_d: Only if the buyer's attorney formally requests it
explanation: RPL 464 requires delivery of the revised statement as soon as practicable, with the duty ending no later than the earlier of transfer of title or buyer occupancy.

question: Under RPL 466, what is a listing agent's duty regarding a seller's Article 14 obligations?
choice_a: To personally complete the Disclosure Statement on the seller's behalf
choice_b: To timely inform the seller of the seller's obligations under Article 14
choice_c: To verify every representation in the statement through independent investigation
choice_d: To deliver a copy of the statement directly to the county clerk
explanation: RPL 466 requires a listing agent to timely inform the seller they represent of the seller's obligations under Article 14 -- not to complete or verify the statement itself.

question: A seller's agent is dealing directly with an unrepresented buyer who has no buyer's agent. Under RPL 466, what duty does the seller's agent owe that buyer regarding Article 14?
choice_a: No duty at all, since the agent represents only the seller
choice_b: A duty to complete the Disclosure Statement on the buyer's behalf
choice_c: The same duty a buyer's agent would owe -- to timely inform the buyer of the buyer's rights and obligations under the Article, before the buyer signs a binding contract of sale
choice_d: A duty limited to disclosing only the environmental section of the statement
explanation: RPL 466 requires the buyer's agent, or the seller's agent when dealing directly with an unrepresented buyer, to timely inform that buyer of the buyer's rights and obligations under Article 14 before the buyer signs a binding contract of sale.

question: A buyer's agent fails to inform the buyer of the buyer's rights under Article 14 before the buyer signs a binding contract of sale. What is the effect under RPL 466?
choice_a: The agent's real estate license is automatically revoked
choice_b: The sale becomes automatically voidable by the buyer
choice_c: The seller becomes solely responsible for the agent's omission, with no other consequence
choice_d: The agent has not performed the required duty and therefore does not receive the Article's liability shield for a violation of the Article
explanation: RPL 466 grants the liability shield only to an agent who performs the required timely-notice duty; an agent who fails to do so does not receive that protection under the Article.

question: Under RPL 443-a, which of the following facts is explicitly deemed NOT to be a material defect requiring disclosure by a seller or agent?
choice_a: That a former occupant of the property died of any cause, including homicide or suicide
choice_b: That the roof has an active leak known to the seller
choice_c: That the foundation has a documented structural crack
choice_d: That the property lacks a valid certificate of occupancy
explanation: RPL 443-a(1)(b) provides that it is not a material defect that a property was the site of a death, including homicide or suicide, or a felony -- unlike genuine physical defects such as a roof leak or foundation crack, which remain disclosable material facts.

question: Under RPL 443-a(3), who is authorized to submit a written inquiry to the seller about a fact unrelated to the physical condition of the property, such as a prior occupant's health status?
choice_a: Any member of the public, at any time, without limitation
choice_b: A buyer who is making or has made a bona fide offer to purchase the property, submitted through the buyer's agent to the seller's agent
choice_c: Only the buyer's attorney, and only after the contract of sale is signed
choice_d: Only a licensed home inspector retained by the buyer
explanation: RPL 443-a(3) allows a buyer making a bona fide offer to submit a written inquiry through the buyer's agent to the seller's agent (or directly to the seller if there is no seller's agent); the seller may then choose whether to respond.
